Learning Objectives
Discuss the concept and importance of the reconstructive ladder (or elevator) metaphor with
regard to planning and execution of microsurgical reconstruction.
Review the four factors necessary for optimal success with microsurgical techniques.
Explain the main microsurgical techniques for anastomosis and their indications.
The Need for Microsurgery
Before the decision is made to pursue a microsurgical treatment option, an effective algorithm
be used to consider reconstructive options.
For replantation, the algorithm addresses the likelihood that the finger or fingers will survive
and be useful.


The Need for Microsurgery
The decision to pursue microsurgical reconstruction is based on considerable thought
and planning. Requisites include a clear understanding of a patient’s deficit, desired
outcome, and willingness and ability to undergo major surgical treatment with its
associated risks (including possible donor site issues), as well as the feasibility and
probability of the patient successfully regaining desired functions. Therefore, surgeons
should have a rough surgical map of the process via which they plan to accomplish the
desired goal. These surgical procedures are multi-step processes (and often multiple
distinct surgical procedures), in which each step affects the subsequent steps.
Metaphors for Planning and Execution
The metaphor itself—whether ladder, elevator, or supermarket—is not as important as
understanding and appropriately applying the components of planning and execution.
Reconstructive Ladder
Metaphor first described by Mathes and Nahai1 in 1982
Options for wound closure should be considered in order from the simplest to the most
complex.

Reconstructive Ladder
Starting with the simplest option and working toward more complex options is not
realistic for some reconstructive needs. For example, thumb reconstruction does not fit
well into the reconstructive ladder metaphor, because even the simple options for
thumb reconstruction require the surgeon to skip multiple lower rungs on the
reconstructive ladder.
Reconstructive Elevator

AAOS | Microsurgery Techniques
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002071
2/15


Reconstructive Elevator
Because microvascular techniques have improved, in the elevator metaphor, surgeons
should directly select the technique they believe will most effectively accomplish the
reconstructive goals. No need exists to start with the least complex option and work
stepwise up the ladder to greater complexity.
Reconstructive Supermarket

Reconstructive Supermarket
Reconstructive options are organized similar to products a supermarket, which are
organized into categories. Rather than considering treatment options from the least
complex to more complex (the reconstructive ladder) or directly selecting a specific
solution (the reconstructive elevator), in the supermarket metaphor, the surgeon
considers the needs and all the reconstructive options that address these needs (Figure
1).
Figure 1 Chart shows the reconstructive grid, which is used to aid the judgement of
reconstructive surgeons. NPWT = negative-pressure wound therapy. (Reproduced with
permission from Mohapatra DP, Thiruvoth FM: Reconstruction 2.0: Restructuring the
reconstructive ladder. Plast Reconstr Surg 2021;147[3]:572e-573e.)

Ablative Versus Restorative Surgery
“Incomplete or confused ablative procedures doom restorative procedures to be
compromised or lost in the underlying disorder”2
Ablative Surgery
Must be adequate and timely
Must precede any restorative surgery
Restorative Surgery
Planning for restorative surgery can be performed only after the surgeon understands the
deficit and the extent of healthy and useful tissue that remains.
The presence of nonviable tissue compromises the viability of remaining tissue.
Successful Microsurgery
Four Major Components of Successful Microsurgery
Preparation of the surgical field, with removal of all nonviable tissue
Identification of the best, reliable, and uninjured recipient vessels
Meticulous elevation of an appropriate flap for the reconstructive need
Design and insetting of the flap in a manner that accomplishes adequate coverage and avoids
pressure on or kinking of the pedicle vessels
Preparation of the Surgical Field: Débridement
Importance cannot be overstated
Governed by two principles and one corollary
Timeliness: Delay of timely débridement allows the retained marginal or dead tissue to lead
to colonization, infection, contracture, and more friable tissues.
Assertiveness of approach: Tissue that looks dead should be removed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Microsurgery Techniques
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002071
4/15

The surgeon should have confidence in removal of clearly nonviable tissue and trust the
coverage options.
The surgeon should not avoid removal of nonviable tissue for fear of more complex
reconstruction.
Reconstructive needs must not affect the decision of tissue that should be débrided versus
retained.
Corollary: If a wound requires more than one or two débridements, then the initial
débridements likely were not sufficiently timely or assertive.
Recipient Vessels
Healthy recipient vessels
No intimal damage should be present; however, the surgeon should resect until no intimal
damage remains.
Stay out of the zone of injury.
The zone of injury is the area that absorbed extreme energy at the time of trauma, injuring
soft and osseous tissue structures.
In blunt trauma, this zone may be quite large.
Although the zone of injury is not always obvious, the surgeon must appreciate the full area
that was injured.
Strong inflow: artery
Strong inflow: pulsatile flow from the recipient vessel that spurts several centimeters
If inflow is not strong, then one of three main causes may be considered.
Normal/non-pathologic vasospasm: normal physiologic spasm that is common in upper
extremities
Caused by being cold in the operating room, manipulation of vessels, mild hypovolemia,
or hypotension
Improves noticeably and quickly if the above factors are corrected and with papaverine
and/or lidocaine administered directly onto the surface of the vessel
Pathologic vasospasm: Zone of injury and/or intimal damage are primary causes.
Thrombus also is associated with zone of injury and/or intimal damage.
Anterograde flow is preferred over retrograde flow
Only under very rare and specific circumstances should the surgeon consider using a
recipient artery with retrograde flow (eg, using a distal radial artery if the proximal radial
artery is nonviable because of the zone of injury).

Use a vessel of as large a caliber as is reasonable for an appropriate size match between
recipient and donor vessels is desirable.
End-to-end anastomosis should be performed if possible.
A good end-to-end anastomosis is preferred over a good end-to-side anastomosis.
A good end-to-side anastomosis is preferred over a bad end-to-end anastomosis (Figure 2).
Vein grafting of the gap should be performed if it is impossible to stay out of the zone of
injury via any of the following three strategies:
Delay: waiting days or weeks before proceeding with microvascular reconstructive surgery
to allow for maximal recovery of the surrounding blood vessels
Débridement
Use of a longer donor vessel
Vein graft should be reversed if used for artery reconstruction.
Vein graft should not be reversed if used for vein reconstruction.
This may seem obvious (because of valves in the vein), but mistakes are commonly made
in both of these situations, especially after a very long procedure with minimal sleep.
Vein graft options from large to small
Saphenous: great option for major named vessels (brachial artery, proximal radial and
ulnar arteries)
Lesser saphenous: good option for smaller named vessels (distal radial and ulnar arteries)
Dorsal foot: palmar arch reconstruction
Volar forearm: good option for common and proper digital artery reconstruction
Venous flow through flap: good option, especially in digits in which a deficiency of artery
and soft-tissue coverage is present
Harvesting involves taking the skin along with the underlying vein.
The technique is straightforward for small flaps but becomes increasingly complex if the
size of the harvested flap increases.
Limb shortening
Should be considered if end-to-end anastomosis is not possible
May be helpful in replantation surgery and complex revascularization procedures
Recipient vein
Ideally two or more per artery
As big as or, ideally, bigger than donor veins

Figure 2 Illustrations show the technique for arteriotomy. Anterior (A) and posterior (B) views
show a tray stitch placed at the site of the arteriotomy. C, Sutures must be placed radial to the
center of the arteriotomy. D, If sutures are placed transversely, leakage will occur at the corners.
Donor Vessels
Replantation
Stay out of zone of injury as much as is possible.
Same rules as those already mentioned apply.
Microvascular reconstruction
Pedicle length should be maximized; additional pedicle length should be attained if possible.
Vessel diameter should be optimized by harvesting as large as possible.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Microsurgery Techniques
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002071
7/15

Insetting
Avoid kinking of the arteries and veins.
The goal during harvesting is a long pedicle but not a redundant pedicle because this leads to
kinking of vessels.
The surgeon can place adipose tissue between vessels to prevent kinking and allow for a
comfortable lie of the vessels.
Inset loosely; no pressure should be on the pedicle with closure.
Exceedingly low threshold for skin graft over any areas that may be slightly tight
Drains: Hematoma is a major cause of pressure.
Excellent hemostasis throughout the entire duration of procedure is necessary to prevent
hematoma.
If any concern with regard to pressure exists, the surgeon can use sutures that can be easily
released postoperatively.
Immobilization of the limb is crucial; flaps can be lost with nonadherence to activity
restrictions.
Elevation should be used to optimize venous outflow but should not be too high because of
arterial inflow considerations.
Insetting of the flap
One of the most technical and underappreciated portions of the surgical procedure
Remember and adhere to the principles previously described.
Postoperative Management
Postoperative swelling is normal and should be anticipated during design and insetting of the
flap.
Monitoring: should occur every 30 minutes for the immediate postoperative period and then
every hour for the first 36 hours postoperatively

Postoperative Management
The patient must be on a surgical floor with nurses familiar and comfortable with
treating patients who have microvascular free flaps. Monitoring should be made as easy
as possible for the nursing staff and junior residents. One technique is to clearly identify
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Microsurgery Techniques
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002071
8/15

the area to be monitored with the use of a 5-0 prolene suture placed loosely in the site
at which a signal detectable via Doppler should be found. In addition, the surgeon
should clearly label any areas at which no pressure should be tolerated. The surgeon
should spend the time in the operating room to appropriately position, dress, label, and
splint the extremity. Although this will occur at the end of the procedure, the process
should not be rushed and should be carried out carefully and thoughtfully. The patient
should be on bed rest for at least the first 24 hours postoperatively, with a Foley catheter
placed if he or she is unable to use a urinal or a bedpan safely. After the first 72-hour
window passes, activity level and monitoring windows can be advanced.
Anticoagulation
The evidence on this topic, discussion of which can fill several pages, primarily consists
of case series and expert opinion. Evidence remains poor, largely because of
heterogeneity of the flaps and surgical management. Patients benefit from some form of
anticoagulation therapy. After microvascular surgery and some degree of injury to the
intima, the anastomotic sites are prothrombotic; however, patients also are at risk for
hematoma and consequent increased pressure on the anastomoses and flap. These two
competing interests—preventing thrombus and preventing excessive bleeding—must be
balanced as well as possible. For elective microsurgical reconstructive procedures, a
common approach is to treat patients via the same regimen used for deep vein
thrombosis prophylaxis. Examples include enoxaparin (40 mg/day), dalteparin (2,500 to
5,000 U/day), and aspirin (80 to 325 mg two times/day).2
Venous outflow
Avoiding flap congestion is crucial for success. Failure in the immediate postoperative
period is most commonly to the result of insufficient arterial inflow; however, in the
perioperative period, inadequate venous outflow is the primary problem and may
manifest slowly. All the aforementioned factors are critical in maintaining adequate
outflow. If venous congestion occurs despite preventative measures, intentional
bleeding from the flap may be the difference between success and failure. The use of
medicinal leeches is the most common method and is observed in digit replantation. If
the flap is small (such as in digit replantation), intentional bleeding, such as that with the
use of leeches, may be a useful technique; however, this is not a practical technique for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:45 PM
AAOS | Microsurgery Techniques
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002071
9/15

medium to large flaps. The key is that the venous outflow must equal the arterial inflow.
If the required arterial inflow to a flap (proportional to the metabolic requirements of a
flap) is high, then the necessary outflow also must be high. The induction of intentional
bleeding in a flap in which arterial inflow is high but venous outflow is low is not feasible.
In these situations, surgeons must resolve the intrinsic venous outflow.
Microvascular Techniques
The specific techniques used are less important than good execution of technique. Any of the
techniques are adequate if performed well; however, if minor missteps with the techniques
occur, then the anastomosis will thrombose.2,3
Approach (Figure 3)
Front wall first
Typical and recommended technique for most vessels
After the front wall is completed, the vessel is flipped, and the back wall is completed.
Back wall first
Important if the vessel cannot be rotated
The back wall is completed first; the surgeon then works up to the front wall.

Figure 3 Photograph shows a microsurgical instrument set. (Courtesy of Pocket Suture, Tucson,
AZ.)
Techniques
Front wall techniques: used if the vessel can be rotated to allow for completion of the back wall
180° techniques
12-o’clock and 6-o’clock positions addressed first, after which sutures are placed between
these two positions
Criticism: Grabbing the back wall on sutures placed in between is possible (Figure 4).

Figure 4 Illustrations shows a 180° front wall microvascular technique. The second half of
the second suture must be placed so that the entry (A) and the exit (B) points are
equidistant from the first suture (C).
120° techniques: described by Acland3
Front wall 1-o’clock and 5-o’clock positions addressed first, after which sutures are placed
between these two positions
Vessel rotated and then suture placed at 9-o’clock position
Complete sutures placed between the 5-o’clock and 9-o’clock positions and the 9-o’clock
and 1-o’clock positions
Suture tails should be left long at 1-o’clock, 5-o’clock, and 9-o’clock positions until sutures
between have been placed
Anastomosis suture and devices
Polypropylene or nylon on tapered needle
9-0 for vessels larger than 2 mm
10-0 for vessels 1 to 2 mm
11-0 for pediatric digital arteries or digital tip replants (<0.8 mm)
Venous couplers
Faster than suture with higher patency rates
Thin-walled vessel is necessary (ie, veins)
Veins must be larger 1.0 mm
Not ideal for superficial system veins because coupler will be palpable (Figure 5)
